# PowerShell standards

> Generated from ai-powershell-standards 2.0.0. Do not edit this file.
> Its source is the `standards` folder of that repository; `Tools/Build-AgentInstructions.ps1` rebuilds it.

These are the rules for writing and reviewing PowerShell in this repository. **MUST** and
**MUST NOT** are requirements. **SHOULD** is the default: depart from it only for a reason you state.

## How to apply the rules

- Apply them to code you write or change. Do not reformat or rewrite code the task does not touch.
- An explicit instruction from the user takes precedence. If following it breaks a MUST, say which
  one. A departure that is meant to stay is recorded in the code (DOC-22). Leave a recorded
  departure as it is, and do not record one that the user has not decided.
- Do not invent facts: no made-up module names, version numbers, measurements, links, or authors. Ask,
  or leave it out.
- When you can run commands, run PSScriptAnalyzer and the tests before you report the work as done,
  and say what you ran.

## Core rules

These are the rules that matter in almost every file. They are a selection from the topic files, and
each one keeps the ID it has there, so the numbers below are not consecutive: STY-04, for example, is
in the style file. The topic files have gaps of their own, because most of them start each section
at a new ten. A gap does not mean that a rule is missing, and a rule that is only in a topic file
counts as much as one listed here.

### Version

- **VER-01** Write for PowerShell 7.6 (LTS) unless the project declares another target. The
  declaration is the project's `#requires -Version` lines and the `PowerShellVersion` and
  `CompatiblePSEditions` keys of its module manifest.
- **VER-02** Write code that also runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1 only when the project declares it:
  `PowerShellVersion = '5.1'`, `CompatiblePSEditions` containing `Desktop`, or
  `#requires -Version 5.1`.
- **VER-04** Code MUST NOT use a command, parameter, operator, or type that the declared target does
  not have. The feature tables in the PowerShell version rules list the ones that differ.
- **VER-06** Commands that exist only in Windows PowerShell MUST NOT be used in code that targets
  PowerShell 7: use `Get-CimInstance` in place of `Get-WmiObject`, and `Get-WinEvent` in place of
  `Get-EventLog`.

### Style

- **STY-02** Use One True Brace Style: an opening brace ends the line that starts the block, a closing
  brace starts its own line, and `else`, `elseif`, `catch`, and `finally` follow that closing brace on
  the same line.
- **STY-03** Lines SHOULD NOT exceed 115 characters. Shorten a long command with splatting, or break
  the line after a pipe, comma, or operator. Backtick line continuation MUST NOT be used.
- **STY-06** Source MUST be ASCII unless a string literal needs another character: no emoji,
  typographic quotes, or en and em dashes in code or comments. Generated documentation and test
  output MUST NOT contain emoji either.
- **STY-12** Name local variables in descriptive camelCase without a type prefix: `$retryCount`, not
  `$RetryCount` or `$intRetryCount`.
- **STY-13** Automatic variables MUST NOT be assigned or reused as parameter, loop, or test-data
  names. The ones most often hit are `$args`, `$input`, `$matches`, `$error`, `$event`, `$host`,
  `$home`, `$pid`, `$profile`, `$sender`, `$this`, `$_`, and `$PSItem`.
- **STY-14** Call commands by their full name with named parameters. Aliases such as `gci`, `ls`,
  `%`, `?`, and `where` MUST NOT be used. One leading positional argument is acceptable where it is
  unambiguous, as in `Write-Verbose 'text'`.
- **STY-16** A local variable MUST NOT have the name of a parameter in any letter case. Variable names
  are case-insensitive, so `$settings = @{}` replaces the value that was passed as `-Settings`.
- **STY-20** Put `$null` on the left of a comparison: `$null -eq $value`.
- **STY-21** Use single quotes for a string that needs no expansion and contains no single quote. In
  an expandable string write `$($object.Property)` for member access, and `${name}` when a colon or
  a name character follows the variable.
- **STY-32** Use `-LiteralPath` whenever the path names one specific item, and always for a path held
  in a variable. `-Path` is for wildcard patterns.
- **STY-40** Build a collection by assigning the output of a loop or pipeline to a variable. An array
  MUST NOT be grown with `+=` inside a loop.
- **STY-42** Wrap a command call in `@()` before the code reads `.Count` or an index from its result,
  or passes the result to a parameter that needs a collection.

### Functions

- **FUN-01** Write every function as an advanced function, with `[CmdletBinding()]` and a `param()`
  block. `$args` MUST NOT be used.
- **FUN-04** `return` in a `begin` block ends only that block; `process` and `end` still run. To stop
  the command there, call `$PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError()`, or set a variable and test it at the
  top of `process`.
- **FUN-10** Declare `[OutputType()]` with the type the function emits. For a custom object, name the
  type as a string and set `PSTypeName` on the object. `[OutputType([PSCustomObject])]` MUST NOT be
  used.
- **FUN-11** Write each object to the pipeline as soon as it is ready. A function MUST NOT collect
  its results in a list and return the list at the end.
- **FUN-12** Only intended output may reach the success stream. Discard a value returned by a method
  or command that is called for its side effect, with `$null = ...` or `[void](...)`.
- **FUN-21** A parameter that accepts pipeline input MUST be handled in a `process` block. Declare it
  as an array and loop over it there, so that pipeline input and a directly passed array behave the
  same way.
- **FUN-25** A function that reduces its pipeline input to one result collects the input in `process`
  and emits the result in `end`, so that piped input and an array argument give the same answer.
- **FUN-26** Read data that came from an API or a file through one accessor that handles both a
  dictionary and an object. Index syntax (`$data['key']`) reads only a dictionary, and member syntax
  (`$data.key`) can return a dictionary's own property instead of the data.
- **FUN-30** A function that changes state MUST declare `SupportsShouldProcess` and guard every change
  with `$PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess()`. Add `ConfirmImpact = 'High'` when the change is destructive.
- **FUN-31** A read-only function, such as one with the verb `Get`, `Test`, or `Find`, MUST NOT
  declare `SupportsShouldProcess`.

### Errors

- **ERR-01** A script that is run directly MUST set `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` and
  `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` immediately after its `param()` block.
- **ERR-02** Module code MUST NOT set `$ErrorActionPreference`, at module scope or inside a function.
  A module sets `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` once, at the top of its `.psm1`.
- **ERR-03** Code MUST run without errors under strict mode: assign a variable before reading it, test
  for an optional property with `$object.PSObject.Properties['Name']`, test for a hashtable key with
  `.ContainsKey()`, and wrap a result in `@()` before reading `.Count` or an index.
- **ERR-10** In an advanced function, put the work that can fail inside `try`, and end the function
  on an unrecoverable failure by calling `$PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError()` in `catch`.
- **ERR-11** `throw` and `Write-Error -ErrorAction Stop` MUST NOT be used in an advanced function. Use
  `throw` only where `$PSCmdlet` does not exist: top-level script code, class methods, and plain
  script blocks.
- **ERR-12** Inside `try`, pass `-ErrorAction Stop` to every command whose failure the `catch` must
  see. A non-terminating error does not enter `catch`.
- **ERR-13** When one input item fails and the rest can still be processed, report the failure with
  `$PSCmdlet.WriteError()` and continue with the next item.
- **ERR-15** Write output to the pipeline after the `try` block, not inside it. An error raised by a
  command further down the pipeline is otherwise caught by this function's `catch`.
- **ERR-20** A `catch` block MUST NOT be empty and MUST NOT hide the error. To tolerate one expected
  failure, catch that exception type and state the reason in a comment.
- **ERR-23** After running a native executable, test `$LASTEXITCODE` and fail when it reports an
  error. A non-zero exit code does not raise a PowerShell error by default.

### Security

- **SEC-01** Secrets MUST NOT appear in source: no passwords, tokens, keys, or connection strings in
  code, parameter defaults, comments, or example values.
- **SEC-03** Accept a credential as a `[PSCredential]` parameter carrying the
  `[System.Management.Automation.Credential()]` attribute. A password MUST NOT be accepted as a
  `[string]` parameter.
- **SEC-05** A function or an unattended script MUST NOT fall back to an interactive prompt
  (`Get-Credential`, `Read-Host`) when a credential or value is missing. It fails with an error that
  names what is missing.
- **SEC-06** Secrets and personal data MUST NOT be written to any stream, log, error message, or
  file. This includes dumping `$PSBoundParameters` or a whole input object.
- **SEC-10** Commands MUST NOT be built from strings: no `Invoke-Expression`, and no
  `[scriptblock]::Create()` on text that includes input. Pass arguments with splatting, or as an
  array for a native executable.

### Help

- **DOC-01** Every function and every script has comment-based help with `.SYNOPSIS`, `.DESCRIPTION`,
  one `.PARAMETER` for each parameter, at least one `.EXAMPLE`, `.INPUTS`, and `.OUTPUTS`.
- **DOC-02** In a function, the help block is the first thing inside the function body, before
  `[CmdletBinding()]`.
- **DOC-05** Help MUST describe what the code does. Performance figures, compliance claims, and
  behaviour that the code does not have MUST NOT be invented. If a fact is not known, leave it out.
- **DOC-07** Help MUST NOT contain a version number, a date, or a change history. An author name is
  added only when the user supplies one or `.github/powershell-attribution.md` lists one (DOC-18).

## Function template

Copy this shape. It runs under strict mode on PowerShell 7.6 and Windows PowerShell 5.1, and its
tests are the test template in `.github/instructions/powershell-pester.instructions.md`.

```powershell
function Get-ConfigValue {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Gets named values from a JSON configuration file.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Reads the JSON file once, then emits one object for each requested name. A name that is
    not in the file is reported as a non-terminating error and the remaining names are still
    processed. A file that cannot be read, or that does not contain a JSON object, is a
    terminating error.

    .PARAMETER Path
    Path of the JSON configuration file. Wildcard characters are not expanded.

    .PARAMETER Name
    One or more top-level property names to read.

    .EXAMPLE
    Get-ConfigValue -Path './settings.json' -Name 'Region'

    Gets the Region value from settings.json.

    .EXAMPLE
    'Region', 'Tier' | Get-ConfigValue -Path './settings.json'

    Gets two values, taking the names from the pipeline.

    .INPUTS
    System.String. You can pipe value names to this function.

    .OUTPUTS
    Example.ConfigValue. An object with Name, Value, and Path properties.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType('Example.ConfigValue')]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$Path,

        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipeline)]
        [string[]]$Name
    )

    begin {
        try {
            $fullPath = Convert-Path -LiteralPath $Path -ErrorAction Stop
            $config = Get-Content -LiteralPath $fullPath -Raw -ErrorAction Stop |
                ConvertFrom-Json -ErrorAction Stop
        } catch {
            $PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($_)
        }

        if ($config -isnot [System.Management.Automation.PSCustomObject]) {
            $exception = [System.IO.InvalidDataException]::new("'$fullPath' does not contain a JSON object.")
            $category = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorCategory]::InvalidData
            $errorRecord = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]::new(
                $exception, 'ConfigNotAnObject', $category, $fullPath)
            $PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($errorRecord)
        }
    }

    process {
        foreach ($item in $Name) {
            $property = $config.PSObject.Properties[$item]
            if ($null -eq $property) {
                $message = "Configuration value '$item' was not found in '$fullPath'."
                $exception = [System.Management.Automation.ItemNotFoundException]::new($message)
                $category = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorCategory]::ObjectNotFound
                $errorRecord = [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]::new(
                    $exception, 'ConfigValueNotFound', $category, $item)
                $PSCmdlet.WriteError($errorRecord)
                continue
            }

            [PSCustomObject]@{
                PSTypeName = 'Example.ConfigValue'
                Name = $property.Name
                Value = $property.Value
                Path = $fullPath
            }
        }
    }
}
```

What the template shows:

- Help is the first thing in the body and covers every parameter, the input, and the output.
- `begin` does the work that must succeed once. Its `catch` ends the function with
  `$PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError($_)`, which keeps the original error.
- A problem the function detects itself becomes an `ErrorRecord` with its own ID and category.
- `process` handles each item. A missing item is reported with `$PSCmdlet.WriteError()` and the loop
  continues, so the caller decides with `-ErrorAction` whether that stops the work.
- Each result is written to the pipeline as it is produced, with a named type, and outside any `try`
  block.
